extracted.intended_audience: media scholars, journalism researchers, and content-analysts studying news selection and foreign newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Content-analytic and theoretical criteria for what makes events 'news' in foreign coverage; includes coding categories, sampling rationale, measurement/indexing methods, and 66 bivariate hypotheses about how news-factors combine. Aimed at studying selection and presentation of foreign news items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: press cutting
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'unit of analysis' is the press cutting as defined by the newspaper (a news story, an editorial, an article, a letter to the editor, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contextual unit is the newspaper itself (e.g. name, party color, date). For each cutting there are 'presentation' variables (layout, length, type, source) and 'proper' variables referring to what is written; each cutting is coded for presence/absence of listed items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual variables vs proper variables
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish contextual variables referring to the newspaper (its name, party color, date) from proper variables that refer to the cutting (presentation, length, type, source) and to what is written.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contextual variables are constant for all units within a paper and used for replication/stratification; proper variables vary across cuttings and are the primary coding targets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling design for newspapers
rubrics_metrics.description: Select newspapers that provide sufficient coverage of foreign news (bigger-city papers), and choose papers to maximize dispersion on relevant axes (e.g. morning/afternoon, radical/conservative) to allow replication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A finding that holds across four different paper types (different political orientation, circulation, format) receives stronger confirmation than a finding from similar papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coding presence/absence (binary item-list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work with a list of items and code a unit according to the presence or absence of these items in the cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many variables are recorded as binary indicators (item present or not); aggregate statistics then report proportions across cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable — Nation (underdog/topdog)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the nation involved in the story as 'underdog/colony' or 'topdog/motherland' (the generic pairings used for Congo–Cuba–Cyprus cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This denotes a difference in rank and a dependence relationship; used to test hypotheses about reporting bias by international rank.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable — People (top leader / elite / rank-and-file / no people)
rubrics_metrics.description: Code the social rank of persons reported or quoted as 'top leader', 'elite', 'rank-and-file', or 'no people'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to assess identification patterns (who is presented) and to relate rank to mode (positive/negative) and quotation frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable — Perspective (east-west, motherland-colony, UN, intra-colony, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Code the perspective or framing of the news story (e.g., East-West, 'motherland-colony', UN-related, intra-colony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Perspective indicates how events are linked to central actors/systems and increases perceived relevance when ties to the center are made explicit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable — Mode of event (negative / positive / neutral / both / neither)
rubrics_metrics.description: Code whether the cutting reports something 'negative' (destruction/disruption), 'positive' (building/constructive), or 'neutral/other'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An index can be computed giving -1 to negative cuttings and +1 to positive ones; average mode values across ranks/cases indicate tendencies toward negativism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable — Focus (economic / political / social / cultural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify the focus of the story by primary domain: economic, political, social, or cultural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to examine whether distant theaters are presented mainly in political/economic terms and to test hypotheses linking focus to distance and relevance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Variable — Source / press agency
rubrics_metrics.description: Record the press agency (AP, UPI, Reuters, AFP, NTB, Tass, own correspondent, others) cited as the source of the cutting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High reliance on a few international agencies implies strong agency-mediated filtering of images; percentages may exceed 100% due to pooled agency attributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsworthiness scoring (additive/complementary combinations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A simple scoring scheme where combinations of factor levels produce a newsworthiness score (e.g., high/high => higher score; low/low => zero).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper distinguishes types (additivity focuses on joint high values; complementarity on when a high Fj compensates for a low Fi); an exclusion hypothesis would focus on mutually exclusive conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measurement: mode index (-1 to +1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composite measure where negative cuttings = -1 and positive = +1; average across cases gives an index between -1 and +1 indicating tendency toward negative or positive framing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Neutral/both/neither are discarded in computing the index; this allows comparison across ranks, nations, and cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complementarity hypothesis (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an event is low on factor Fi, it must be high on some other factor Fj to make news: 'for a low Fi the probability that any Fj is high is greater than for a high Fi'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to bivariate and multivariate hypotheses about how pairs (and higher combinations) of factors jointly determine newsworthiness; motivates testing many two-factor pairings (66 hypotheses from 12 factors).

rubrics_metrics.name: H1 — Distance of nation → elite focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant the nation (cultural distance), the higher the tendency to report elite action (top leaders and elites rather than rank-and-file).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: cultural distance reduces identification with rank-and-file; distant events must present obvious elite actions to be newsworthy; tested across crises.

rubrics_metrics.name: H2 — Rank of person → negativity of event
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the person reported, the more negative the event in which they appear (common people are more often presented in negative contexts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirically measured by counting negative vs. positive contexts by rank; confirmed in many cases (e.g., 23/27 relationships in study in expected direction).

rubrics_metrics.name: H (causal agent rank) — lower-rank causal agents less likely to be seen positively
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the causal agent of an event, the lower the chance that he/she is seen in a context of something positive happening.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Checked by pooling top leader and elite vs rank-and-file and analyzing whether causes are attributed positively or negatively; confirmed in study.

rubrics_metrics.name: H (distance → negativity) — nation distance and negativity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant the nation, the more negative the event (i.e., remote nations appear more often as causes/subjects of negative events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors found no clear confirmation in their data; cultural distance interacts with other factors and everyday reporting from 'mother countries' can counterbalance this effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: H (cultural distance → required relevance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The more culturally distant the theater, the more relevant (to core interests) an event must appear to be included as news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remote events must be linked to familiar groupings (East/West, motherland, UN) or be sensational to pass filters; otherwise they remain unreported.

rubrics_metrics.name: (1,4) — Distance requires frequency condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant a nation is, the more will an event have to satisfy the frequency criterion (i.e., be abrupt or discrete enough to capture attention).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: distant news emphasizes sudden disasters, coups, big qualitative changes — producing images of unpredictability and danger; slow build-ups go underreported.

rubrics_metrics.name: (4,3) — Distance requires low ambiguity
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant an event, the less ambiguous it must be to make news (simplicity preferred for remote events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remote events are presented as 'ideal types' and sweeping generalizations; complex, internally nuanced accounts are reserved for culturally proximate countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: (4,5) — Distance requires consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: The more distant the nation, the more consonant the news must be with existing expectations or stereotypes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Events that fit stereotyped expectations (e.g., coups in certain regions) pass filters more easily; atypical positive or counter-stereotypical stories may be dismissed as anomalies or propaganda.

rubrics_metrics.name: (7,2) — Continuity effect lowers threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher the continuity effect (once event 'makes it' to news), the lower the threshold for follow-up coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Creates 'news strings' and artificial continuities because once the channel is open, subsequent related items require less to be reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: (8,2) — Composition effect lowers threshold
rubrics_metrics.description: The higher the composition effect (need to represent under-represented categories), the lower the threshold for items to be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When little else happens abroad, editors may include lower-scoring items to fill perceived compositional gaps, producing discontinuous images.

rubrics_metrics.name: (1,12) — Positive events need frequency condition
rubrics_metrics.description: The less negative (more positive) the news, the more important the frequency condition: positive events must be short/ceremonial to be reportable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive developments often require elite involvement and staged events (PR), leading to underreporting of slow, grassroots positive change.

rubrics_metrics.name: (9,4) — Low-rank nations must be culturally proximate
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the international rank of a nation, the lower must the cultural distance be for it to be reported (topdog nations have favored underlings geographically/culturally).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Topdog nations tend to over-report from their spheres of influence (U.S.–Latin America, U.K.–Commonwealth), reinforcing existing world divisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: (9,5) — Low-rank nations require consonance
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the nation, the more consonant (stereotype-fitting) the news must be to get reported.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low-rank nations are typically portrayed in terms of 'immaturity' or instability; positive counter-stereotypical developments often go unreported.

rubrics_metrics.name: (10,6) — Low-rank persons require unexpectedness
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the person, the more unexpected the news must be for them to make the story (rank-and-file only make news when something markedly atypical happens).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinary positive actions by common people rarely meet criteria of frequency, threshold, unexpectedness, and continuity; exceptions include sports/arts which may compensate.

rubrics_metrics.name: (9,10) — Low-rank nations require higher-ranking persons to make news
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the nation, the higher the person (within that nation) must be to make news in foreign coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leads to elite-dominated images of underdog nations and poor visibility for mass/popular life there.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-rank nation → predominance of negative reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of the nation, the more negative will the news from that nation have to be (positive developments are underreported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Produces an image of underdog nations as unable to govern themselves and reinforces hierarchical perceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: (10,12) — Low-rank persons must do more negative acts
rubrics_metrics.description: The lower the rank of a person, the more negative his/her actions must be for them to make news (criminality and misfortune more likely to be reported).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive everyday actions by common people rarely fit news criteria unless they are exceptional or framed as events (lottery wins, catastrophes).

rubrics_metrics.name: (11,12) — Non-personal events must be negative
rubrics_metrics.description: The less personal the news (i.e., events not attributed to people), the more negative they have to be to appear in the news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positive developments are more likely to be attributed to people; impersonal phenomena (natural disasters) must be negative to qualify as news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presentation indicators of 'seriousness'
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic presentation features (morning vs afternoon paper layout, use of headlines, vocabulary) indicate a 'serious' paper and are relevant contextual variables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider presentation variables when stratifying samples or interpreting differences in coverage style and depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication principle in sampling
rubrics_metrics.description: Select diverse papers so that consistent findings across them give higher confirmation than findings replicated in similar papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design the sample to include different axes (political color, circulation, morning/afternoon) to test robustness across newsroom types.
